name: Chapter 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination
description: Nitrogenous wastes, excretory organs, kidney and nephron, urine formation, counter current, regulation, micturition, disorders

cards.definition: Ammonia, urea, uric acid

cards.term: Most and least toxic nitrogenous waste?
cards.definition: Most toxic: ammonia (needs lots of water). Least toxic: uric acid (minimum water loss).

Ammonotelic (ammonia): Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects; Ureotelic (urea): Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes; Uricotelic (uric acid): Reptiles, birds, land snails, insects

Ammonotelic (ammonia)Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
Ureotelic (urea)Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes
Uricotelic (uric acid)Reptiles, birds, land snails, insects

cards.definition: By diffusion across body surfaces or gills as ammonium ions; kidneys play no significant role

cards.term: Why are terrestrial animals ureotelic or uricotelic, not ammonotelic?
cards.definition: To conserve water: urea and uric acid are less toxic and need less water to remove

cards.term: Where is ammonia converted to urea?
cards.definition: In the liver

cards.term: Why do some animals retain urea in the kidney matrix?
cards.definition: To maintain a desired osmolarity

cards.term: In what form do uricotelic animals excrete uric acid?
cards.definition: As a pellet or paste
"Birds and Reptiles Save Water": birds, reptiles, land snails and insects excrete uric acid

Protonephridia (flame cells): Flatworms (Planaria), rotifers, some annelids, Amphioxus; Nephridia: Earthworm, other annelids; Malpighian tubules: Most insects (cockroach); Antennal (green) glands: Crustaceans (prawn); Kidneys: Vertebrates

cards.definition: Osmoregulation (ionic and fluid volume regulation)
Amphioxus (cephalochordate)
Regulation of water and ionic balance of body fluids

cards.term: Parts of the human excretory system?
cards.definition: A pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra
Between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity

cards.term: Size and weight of an adult kidney?
cards.definition: 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick; 120–170 g
A notch on the inner concave surface through which ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter
A broad funnel-shaped space inner to the hilum, with projections called calyces
Outer cortex and inner medulla
Conical masses of the medulla projecting into the calyces

cards.term: What are the columns of Bertini?
cards.definition: Extensions of the cortex between medullary pyramids (renal columns)

cards.term: Functional unit of the kidney, and how many per kidney?
cards.definition: Nephron; nearly one million
Glomerulus and renal tubule
A tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole
Afferent (from renal artery) brings blood to the glomerulus; efferent carries it away
Afferent = Arrives; Efferent = Exits
A double-walled cup at the start of the renal tubule, enclosing the glomerulus

cards.term: What is the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)?
cards.definition: Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule

cards.text: Renal tubule: Bowman's capsule → {{c1::PCT}} → {{c2::Henle's loop}} (descending, ascending limbs) → {{c3::DCT}} → {{c4::collecting duct}} → renal pelvis.

cards.term: Which parts of the nephron lie in the cortex, and which dip into the medulla?
cards.definition: Cortex: Malpighian corpuscle, PCT, DCT. Medulla: loop of Henle.
Cortical (majority): short loop, barely enters medulla. Juxtamedullary: long loop, deep into medulla.
A fine capillary network formed by the efferent arteriole around the renal tubule
A minute U-shaped vessel of the peritubular network running parallel to Henle's loop

cards.term: In which nephrons is the vasa recta absent or reduced?
cards.definition: Cortical nephrons

masks.answer: Descending limb of loop of Henle
Ascending limb of loop of Henle

cards.term: How much blood do the kidneys filter per minute?
cards.definition: 1100–1200 mL: about 1/5 of cardiac output

cards.term: Three layers of the filtration membrane?
cards.definition: Endothelium of glomerular vessels, epithelium of Bowman's capsule, and a basement membrane between them
Epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule, arranged to leave filtration slits (slit pores)

cards.term: Why is glomerular filtration called ultrafiltration?
cards.definition: Filtering is so fine that all plasma constituents except proteins pass into Bowman's capsule
Glomerular capillary blood pressure

cards.term: Why is glomerular blood pressure high? (intuition)
cards.definition: The efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent, so blood backs up in the glomerulus like a nozzle
Amount of filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute: about 125 mL/min = 180 L/day
Juxtaglomerular apparatus: a sensitive region formed by cellular modifications of the DCT and afferent arteriole where they touch

cards.term: How does the JGA restore a falling GFR?
cards.definition: JG cells release renin, which raises glomerular blood flow and GFR

cards.term: Filtrate per day vs urine per day?
cards.definition: 180 L vs 1.5 L: nearly 99% is reabsorbed

cards.term: Which substances are reabsorbed actively vs passively?
cards.definition: Active: glucose, amino acids, Na⁺. Passive: nitrogenous wastes, water (in initial segments).

cards.term: What is secreted by tubular cells?
cards.definition: H⁺, K⁺, ammonia
Maintains ionic and acid-base balance of body fluids
Simple cuboidal brush border epithelium: more surface area for reabsorption

cards.term: What is reabsorbed in the PCT?
cards.definition: Nearly all essential nutrients and 70–80% of electrolytes and water

cards.term: How does the PCT maintain pH?
cards.definition: Secretes H⁺ and ammonia into the filtrate and absorbs HCO₃⁻

cards.term: Descending limb of Henle's loop: permeability?
cards.definition: Permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes → filtrate becomes concentrated

cards.term: Ascending limb of Henle's loop: permeability?
cards.definition: Impermeable to water, allows electrolyte transport → filtrate becomes dilute

cards.text: The ascending limb of Henle's loop is {{c1::impermeable}} to water, whereas the descending limb is {{c2::permeable}} to it.

cards.definition: Maintaining high osmolarity of the medullary interstitial fluid (reabsorption is minimal in the ascending limb)
Conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water; reabsorbs HCO₃⁻; secretes H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ (pH and Na–K balance)
Reabsorbs large amounts of water (concentrated urine); passes some urea to the medulla; secretes H⁺ and K⁺
In the PCT (actively)
Henle's loop and vasa recta

cards.term: Why is it called counter current?
cards.definition: Filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop, and blood in the two limbs of vasa recta, flow in opposite directions
From 300 mOsmol/L in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol/L in the inner medulla

cards.term: Which two solutes cause the medullary gradient?
cards.definition: NaCl and urea

cards.term: Path of NaCl in the counter current mechanism?
cards.definition: Ascending limb of Henle → exchanged with descending vasa recta → returned to interstitium by ascending vasa recta

cards.term: Path of urea in the counter current mechanism?
cards.definition: Small amounts enter the thin ascending limb of Henle's loop; returned to the interstitium by the collecting tubule

cards.term: How does the medullary gradient concentrate urine?
cards.definition: Water leaves the collecting duct easily into the hyperosmotic interstitium

cards.term: How concentrated can human urine be?
cards.definition: Nearly four times the initial filtrate (300 → 1200 mOsmol/L)

cards.term: Kidney function is regulated by feedback involving?
cards.definition: The hypothalamus, JGA and, to some extent, the heart
Changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration

cards.term: What happens on excessive fluid loss?
cards.definition: Osmoreceptors → hypothalamus → ADH (vasopressin) released from the neurohypophysis
Increases water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis; also constricts vessels, raising BP and GFR

cards.term: True or false: ADH helps in water elimination, making urine hypotonic.
cards.definition: False. ADH conserves water and makes urine concentrated (hypertonic).
Fall in GFR → JG cells release renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction ↑ BP; also aldosterone from adrenal cortex
Powerful vasoconstrictor (↑ glomerular BP, GFR); stimulates aldosterone release
Reabsorption of Na⁺ and water from distal parts of the tubule → ↑ BP and GFR

cards.term: What is ANF, and when is it released?
cards.definition: Atrial natriuretic factor: released by the heart atria when blood flow to them increases
Vasodilation → lowers BP; acts as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism
ADH: Raises (water retained, vessels constricted); Angiotensin II: Raises (vasoconstriction); Aldosterone: Raises (Na⁺ and water retained); ANF: Lowers (vasodilation)

cards.definition: The process of release of urine
Bladder stretches → stretch receptors signal CNS → CNS makes bladder smooth muscle contract and urethral sphincter relax

cards.term: Urine per day in an adult?
cards.definition: 1–1.5 L
Light yellow, watery, slightly acidic (pH 6.0), characteristic odour
25–30 g

cards.term: What are glycosuria and ketonuria? What do they indicate?
cards.definition: Glucose and ketone bodies in urine; indicate diabetes mellitus

cards.term: Organs other than kidneys that help in excretion?
cards.definition: Lungs, liver, skin (and a little via saliva)
About 200 mL CO₂/min and significant water

cards.term: What does the liver excrete through bile?
cards.definition: Bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins, drugs
Water, NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid
Cooling the body surface
Sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes via sebum (protective oily covering)
Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction
Blood from an artery + heparin → dialysing unit (coiled cellophane tube in dialysing fluid) → wastes diffuse out → anti-heparin added → returned via a vein

cards.term: Dialysing fluid contains everything in plasma except?
cards.definition: The nitrogenous wastes

cards.term: Why is heparin added before dialysis and anti-heparin after?
cards.definition: Heparin stops clotting in the machine; anti-heparin restores normal clotting before blood returns

cards.term: Ultimate treatment for acute renal failure?
cards.definition: Kidney transplantation, preferably from a close relative to minimise rejection
Kidney stones: insoluble crystallised salts (oxalates) formed in the kidney
Inflammation of the glomeruli
Ammonotelism: Bony fish; Bowman's capsule: Renal tubule; Micturition: Urinary bladder; Uricotelism: Birds; ADH: Water reabsorption
